In [[mathematics]], the '''multiple orthogonal polynomials''' ('''MOPs''') are [[orthogonal polynomials]] in one variable that are [[orthogonal]] with respect to a finite family of [[Measure (mathematics)|measure]]s. The polynomials are divided into two classes named ''type 1'' and ''type 2''.<ref>López-Lagomasino, G. (2021). An Introduction to Multiple Orthogonal Polynomials and Hermite-Padé Approximation. In: Marcellán, F., Huertas, E.J. (eds) Orthogonal Polynomials: Current Trends and Applications. SEMA SIMAI Springer Series, vol 22. Springer, Cham. https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-030-56190-1_9</ref>

In the literature, MOPs are also called ''<math>d</math>-orthogonal polynomials'', ''Hermite-Padé polynomials'' or ''polyorthogonal polynomials''. MOPs should not be confused with multivariate orthogonal polynomials.
==Multiple orthogonal polynomials==
Consider a [[multiindex]] <math>\vec{n}=(n_1,\dots,n_r)\in \mathbb{N}^r</math> and <math>r</math> positive measures <math>\mu_1,\dots,\mu_r</math> over the reals. As usual <math>|\vec{n}|:=n_1+n_2+\cdots + n_r</math>.
=== MOP of type 1 ===
Polynomials <math>A_{\vec{n},j}</math> for <math>j=1,2,\dots,r</math> are of ''type 1'' if the <math>j</math>-th polynomial <math>A_{\vec{n},j}</math> has at most degree <math>n_j-1</math> such that
:<math>\sum\limits_{j=1}^r\int_{\R}x^kA_{\vec{n},j}d\mu_j(x)=0,\qquad k=0,1,2,\dots,|\vec{n}|-2,</math>
and
:<math>\sum\limits_{j=1}^r\int_{\R}x^{|\vec{n}|-1}A_{\vec{n},j}d\mu_j(x)=1.</math><ref name="Ismail">{{cite book|title=Classical and Quantum Orthogonal Polynomials in One Variable|first1=Mourad E. H.|last1=Ismail|publisher=Cambridge University Press|date=2005|isbn=9781107325982|pages=607-608}}</ref>

====Explanation====
This defines a system of <math>|\vec{n}|</math> equations for the <math>|\vec{n}|</math> coefficients of the polynomials <math>A_{\vec{n},1},A_{\vec{n},2},\dots,A_{\vec{n},r}</math>.

===MOP of type 2===
A monic polynomial <math>P_{\vec{n}}(x)</math> is of ''type 2'' if it has degree <math>|\vec{n}|</math> such that
:<math>\int_{\R}P_{\vec{n}}(x)x^k d\mu_j(x)=0,\qquad k=0,1,2,\dots,n_j-1,\qquad j=1,\dots,r.</math><ref name="Ismail" />
====Explanation====
If we write <math>j=1,\dots,r</math> out, we get the following definition
:<math>\int_{\R}P_{\vec{n}}(x)x^k d\mu_1(x)=0,\qquad k=0,1,2,\dots,n_1-1</math>
:<math>\int_{\R}P_{\vec{n}}(x)x^k d\mu_2(x)=0,\qquad k=0,1,2,\dots,n_2-1</math>
:<math>\vdots</math>
:<math>\int_{\R}P_{\vec{n}}(x)x^k d\mu_r(x)=0,\qquad k=0,1,2,\dots,n_r-1</math>
